analysis.one_liner: Bans 'forever chemicals' (PFAS) in food packaging like wrappers and takeout containers.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban PFAS from food packaging was introduced in September 2024 with 23 House supporters, but never received a hearing or vote before the term ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sell food packaging containing PFAS — man-made 'forever chemicals' that don't break down in the body or environment and have been linked to health problems. It adds PFAS packaging to the list of banned food adulterants under the federal food safety law, with the ban taking effect January 1, 2025. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who eat packaged, carry-out, and fast food, since PFAS coatings on wrappers and containers can transfer into food. It also benefits people exposed down the chain — food-contact-paper plant workers and communities near landfills or water supplies contaminated by these chemicals — because a ban cuts PFAS out of the packaging stream at the source.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to prohibit introducing into interstate commerce any food packaging containing intentionally added PFAS, defined as man-made per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom. [S2]
The ban applies beginning January 1, 2025, giving PFAS used in grease-proofing on fast-food wrappers, takeout containers, and other food contact materials an explicit federal prohibition. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies that make PFAS grease-proofing agents and food-packaging manufacturers would have to reformulate or switch to PFAS-free alternatives, with some cost passed through to restaurants and ultimately consumers. FDA would also gain a new enforcement responsibility.

drawbacks.text: The ban took effect January 1, 2025 — a little over three months after introduction — leaving packaging suppliers and small food businesses very little runway to find and certify PFAS-free alternatives. [S2]

A blanket ban covers the entire huge class of PFAS compounds regardless of individual chemical's tested behavior, which some manufacturers argue removes any risk-based assessment; several states, however, have already adopted similar bans on food packaging, showing the approach is administrable. [S2]
PFAS-free grease-resistant alternatives can cost more, a cost that would flow through restaurants and grocery margins to consumers, though the amounts are small per package.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health gain — cutting a persistent, accumulating chemical out of direct food contact — is large relative to the cost of switching to alternatives that already exist and are already required by several state laws. The main legitimate criticism is the abrupt effective date rather than the ban itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the congressional term ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on September 27, 2024, with 22 original cosponsors, including one Republican, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick. [S2][S3]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which was the bill's only committee action. [S4]
No further action appears in the record; the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS producers and food-packaging suppliers avoided a compliance deadline, and nothing changed for consumers — PFAS remained legal in federally regulated food packaging, though several states already ban it on their own.

for.name: Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 22 original cosponsors. [S2][S4]

for.name: Brian Fitzpatrick
for.role: U.S. Representative (PA), the sole Republican cosponsor

for.name: 21 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: House Democrats including Norton, Grijalva, Tlaib, Schakowsky, McGovern, Nadler, and Lofgren

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA) in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and the bill died in committee. [S4]

against.name: PFAS chemical and packaging manufacturers
against.role: Producers of fluorochemicals and food-contact packaging
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal PFAS restrictions during this period; the bill received no committee action despite state-level bans moving in several states.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors were Democrats except one Republican, Brian Fitzpatrick; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: A federal ban on PFAS in food packaging eliminates a market for PFAS grease-proofing agents. Their interest in avoiding restrictions runs against consumers' interest in less chemical exposure through food.

industries.industry: Food-contact packaging makers (paper and fast-food packaging)
industries.note: They would bear reformulation and sourcing costs on a short timeline, but PFAS-free coatings exist and several states already require them, so the burden is a compliance cost rather than an existential threat. Consumers currently pay the cost of the status quo in chemical exposure instead.
They would face supply-switching costs but benefit from clearer federal rules than a patchwork of differing state bans.
